quests.hint: 'Had... been published' is the passive form of the inverted third conditional.
quests.explanation: This combines the inverted third conditional with the passive voice, since the theory itself is the focus, not who published it. Layering these advanced structures together is genuinely challenging, even for confident speakers.
quests.textToSpeak: Had a well-known scientific theory been published a decade earlier, the public reaction might have looked entirely different at the time.
quests.correctAnswer: Had a well-known scientific theory been published a decade earlier, the public reaction might have looked entirely different at the time.

quests.hint: 'Looking back' is inserted mid-sentence, adding a reflective, thoughtful pause.
quests.explanation: 'Now-accepted' is a compound adjective showing something once doubted has since become widely believed. 'Just how' adds emphasis before an adjective, similar to 'how very'.
quests.textToSpeak: It's easy to forget, looking back, just how controversial some now-accepted scientific ideas once were to ordinary people.
quests.correctAnswer: It's easy to forget, looking back, just how controversial some now-accepted scientific ideas once were to ordinary people.

quests.hint: 'More than once' is inserted mid-sentence, showing this pattern has repeated.
quests.explanation: This cleft sentence, starting with 'What', contrasts past dismissal with present acceptance. 'More than once' inserted mid-sentence adds emphasis, showing this isn't a single unusual case.
quests.textToSpeak: What was once dismissed as impossible by respected experts has, more than once, quietly become common knowledge within a single generation.
quests.correctAnswer: What was once dismissed as impossible by respected experts has, more than once, quietly become common knowledge within a single generation.

quests.hint: 'So often has... turned out' inverts 'has' and the subject after 'so often'.
quests.explanation: 'Turned out to be' describes how something was eventually revealed to be true, often unexpectedly. 'Serve someone well' is an idiom meaning to benefit or help someone effectively.
quests.textToSpeak: So often has confident expert prediction turned out to be wrong that a little humility tends to serve forecasters rather well.
quests.correctAnswer: So often has confident expert prediction turned out to be wrong that a little humility tends to serve forecasters rather well.

quests.hint: 'Yet' here works like 'but', introducing an ironic contrast.
quests.explanation: 'Yet' can introduce a contrast, similar to 'but', often with a note of irony as it does here. 'Built on doing exactly that' refers back to the previous idea without repeating it in full.
quests.textToSpeak: Nobody can predict the future with any real precision, yet entire industries continue to be built on doing exactly that.
quests.correctAnswer: Nobody can predict the future with any real precision, yet entire industries continue to be built on doing exactly that.

quests.hint: 'Bet everything on' is a figurative expression meaning to rely completely on one outcome.
quests.explanation: 'Bet everything on something' figuratively describes taking a large risk based on a single expected outcome, borrowed from gambling. This sentence offers a genuinely practical piece of advice about planning under uncertainty.
quests.textToSpeak: It might be more useful to prepare for several possible futures than to bet everything on getting one single prediction right.
quests.correctAnswer: It might be more useful to prepare for several possible futures than to bet everything on getting one single prediction right.

quests.hint: 'Strikes out of nowhere' personifies creativity as something sudden and external.
quests.explanation: 'Strike out of nowhere' personifies an abstract idea, creativity, as if it were a sudden, external event. The semicolon then contrasts this myth with a more grounded, realistic explanation.
quests.textToSpeak: Creativity rarely strikes out of nowhere; it tends to emerge from long, unglamorous hours of unremarkable, ordinary practice.
quests.correctAnswer: Creativity rarely strikes out of nowhere; it tends to emerge from long, unglamorous hours of unremarkable, ordinary practice.

quests.hint: 'Overshadow' means to make something else seem less important or visible.
quests.explanation: 'Overshadow' describes one idea dominating attention at the expense of another, often unfairly. 'Just how much' emphasises the true, often underestimated scale of something.
quests.textToSpeak: The romantic idea of sudden inspiration tends to overshadow just how much quiet, patient revision most good work actually requires.
quests.correctAnswer: The romantic idea of sudden inspiration tends to overshadow just how much quiet, patient revision most good work actually requires.

quests.hint: 'In reality' is inserted mid-sentence to contrast appearance with truth.
quests.explanation: 'The product of' means the result of, often used for something built up gradually over time. This sentence contrasts surface appearance with underlying reality, a recurring theme throughout this level.
quests.textToSpeak: So much of what looks effortless from the outside is, in reality, the product of years of largely invisible practice.
quests.correctAnswer: So much of what looks effortless from the outside is, in reality, the product of years of largely invisible practice.

quests.hint: 'Globalisation' is stressed on its fourth syllable: glo-ba-li-SA-tion.
quests.explanation: 'Globalisation' describes the increasing connection between economies and cultures worldwide, spelled with an 's' in British English. 'At a cost' figuratively means with a downside, not necessarily a financial one.
quests.textToSpeak: Globalisation has made it possible to enjoy produce from the other side of the world, often at a genuine environmental cost.
quests.correctAnswer: Globalisation has made it possible to enjoy produce from the other side of the world, often at a genuine environmental cost.

quests.hint: 'Supply chain' is a fixed phrase — say the two words smoothly together.
quests.explanation: 'Supply chain' refers to the entire process of producing and delivering goods, now common vocabulary since recent global disruptions. 'A matter of days' emphasises how quickly something now happens, in contrast to the past.
quests.textToSpeak: A single supply chain disruption can now ripple across continents in a matter of days, rather than the weeks it once took.
quests.correctAnswer: A single supply chain disruption can now ripple across continents in a matter of days, rather than the weeks it once took.

quests.hint: 'Given how' introduces a reason based on an already accepted fact.
quests.explanation: 'Given how' introduces a justification based on something already understood to be true, similar to 'given that'. 'Interconnected' describes things closely linked and dependent on one another.
quests.textToSpeak: What happens in one distant market rarely stays contained there for long, given how interconnected modern economies have become.
quests.correctAnswer: What happens in one distant market rarely stays contained there for long, given how interconnected modern economies have become.

quests.hint: 'Shifting subtly' describes a small, gradual, easily missed kind of change.
quests.explanation: 'Subtly' describes a change so gradual or slight it's easily overlooked. This sentence lists three separate factors, 'context, company, and circumstance', each beginning with the same letter for a pleasing rhythm.
quests.textToSpeak: Identity has never been quite as fixed as people sometimes assume, shifting subtly depending on context, company, and circumstance.
quests.correctAnswer: Identity has never been quite as fixed as people sometimes assume, shifting subtly depending on context, company, and circumstance.

quests.hint: The list of three settings, 'work... home... old friends', keeps a steady, even rhythm.
quests.explanation: 'Somewhat differently' softens a claim about change, avoiding an exaggerated 'completely differently'. 'Without ever really thinking of it as' shows this behaviour happens automatically, not through conscious calculation.
quests.textToSpeak: Most people behave somewhat differently at work, at home, and among old friends, without ever really thinking of it as dishonest.
quests.correctAnswer: Most people behave somewhat differently at work, at home, and among old friends, without ever really thinking of it as dishonest.

quests.hint: 'Rather than' at the start contrasts two different ways of understanding identity.
quests.explanation: 'Rather than' at the beginning of a sentence sets up a contrast that's resolved in the second half. 'Roles worn at different times' extends a clothing metaphor, seen earlier with 'history wearing different clothes'.
quests.textToSpeak: Rather than being a single fixed thing, identity might be better understood as several overlapping roles worn at different times.
quests.correctAnswer: Rather than being a single fixed thing, identity might be better understood as several overlapping roles worn at different times.

quests.hint: 'Under conditions of' is a formal way to introduce a specific situation or context.
quests.explanation: 'Under conditions of' is a formal opening phrase common in careful, analytical writing. 'Can itself become' shows an action intended to reduce risk paradoxically creating a new one.
quests.textToSpeak: Under conditions of genuine uncertainty, waiting for complete information before deciding can itself quietly become the riskier choice.
quests.correctAnswer: Under conditions of genuine uncertainty, waiting for complete information before deciding can itself quietly become the riskier choice.

quests.hint: 'So rarely do we have' inverts 'do' and 'we' after 'so rarely'.
quests.explanation: 'Partial information' means incomplete facts, the opposite of having a full picture. This sentence continues the 'so... that...' inversion pattern with a genuinely useful, practical observation.
quests.textToSpeak: So rarely do we have all the facts before deciding that acting on partial information becomes a genuine skill.
quests.correctAnswer: So rarely do we have all the facts before deciding that acting on partial information becomes a genuine skill.

quests.hint: 'Realistically' is inserted mid-sentence, softening an otherwise blunt claim.
quests.explanation: 'Realistically' inserted mid-sentence adds a grounded, practical tone to an otherwise abstract idea. 'Otherwise reasonable' shows the decision is generally sound, aside from the single issue being discussed.
quests.textToSpeak: It's tempting to wait for certainty that may, realistically, never actually arrive before making an otherwise reasonable decision.
quests.correctAnswer: It's tempting to wait for certainty that may, realistically, never actually arrive before making an otherwise reasonable decision.

quests.hint: 'Strip away' means to remove completely, often something valuable.
quests.explanation: 'Strip away' describes removing something, often leaving a situation worse off as a result. 'Get misread as' describes an unintended, mistaken interpretation of something.
quests.textToSpeak: Written messages strip away tone of voice almost entirely, which is precisely why so many texts get misread as rude.
quests.correctAnswer: Written messages strip away tone of voice almost entirely, which is precisely why so many texts get misread as rude.

quests.hint: 'Land as' means to be received or interpreted as, not a literal landing.
quests.explanation: 'Land as' figuratively describes how a message is ultimately received, regardless of its original intention. 'Emotional weight' is a figurative expression for how much feeling something carries.
quests.textToSpeak: A perfectly friendly message can land as cold or sarcastic simply because punctuation carries far more emotional weight than most people realise.
quests.correctAnswer: A perfectly friendly message can land as cold or sarcastic simply because punctuation carries far more emotional weight than most people realise.

quests.hint: 'Spiral into' suggests something growing quickly out of control.
quests.explanation: 'Spiral into something' describes a situation escalating quickly, often for the worse, borrowed from the image of a spinning downward path. This cleft-style sentence again contrasts a simple alternative with a needlessly complicated reality.
quests.textToSpeak: What would take ten seconds to clarify on a phone call can sometimes spiral into a lengthy, entirely avoidable misunderstanding by text.
quests.correctAnswer: What would take ten seconds to clarify on a phone call can sometimes spiral into a lengthy, entirely avoidable misunderstanding by text.

quests.hint: 'Conflating' means mistakenly treating two different things as one.
quests.explanation: 'Conflate' means to combine two separate things as though they were the same, often leading to confusion. This sentence draws a subtle but genuinely useful distinction about the nature of fulfilling work.
quests.textToSpeak: Meaningful work isn't necessarily the same as enjoyable work, and conflating the two can quietly lead to real disappointment.
quests.correctAnswer: Meaningful work isn't necessarily the same as enjoyable work, and conflating the two can quietly lead to real disappointment.

quests.hint: 'Frankly' is inserted mid-sentence, signalling an honest, undecorated admission.
quests.explanation: 'Frankly' inserted mid-sentence signals the speaker is being unusually honest, even if the truth is slightly unflattering. 'Rarely makes it into' means it's rarely mentioned or included, a natural extension of the verb 'make'.
quests.textToSpeak: Some of the most fulfilling work is, frankly, tedious a lot of the time, which rarely makes it into anyone's career advice.
quests.correctAnswer: Some of the most fulfilling work is, frankly, tedious a lot of the time, which rarely makes it into anyone's career advice.

quests.hint: 'Has less to do with X than with Y' redirects a common assumption.
quests.explanation: 'Have less to do with X than with Y' gently corrects an assumption by shifting emphasis toward a subtler explanation. 'Sustains' means to keep something going over time, stronger than simply 'helps'.
quests.textToSpeak: What sustains people through difficult work often has less to do with passion than with a quieter sense of purpose.
quests.correctAnswer: What sustains people through difficult work often has less to do with passion than with a quieter sense of purpose.

quests.hint: 'Confident but ultimately unfocused' pairs a positive quality with a limiting one.
quests.explanation: 'Confident but ultimately unfocused' uses 'but' to pair an apparent strength with a real weakness. 'Uncover' means to reveal something previously hidden, slightly more vivid than 'find'.
quests.textToSpeak: A well-designed question can uncover more useful information than an hour of confident but ultimately unfocused conversation.
quests.correctAnswer: A well-designed question can uncover more useful information than an hour of confident but ultimately unfocused conversation.

quests.hint: 'So valuable is the skill' inverts 'is' and 'the skill' after 'so valuable'.
quests.explanation: This is the final example in this set of the 'so + adjective' inversion pattern, applied to the value of good questions. 'Discipline' here means a formal field or subject of study, not punishment.
quests.textToSpeak: So valuable is the skill of asking a genuinely good question that entire fields now teach it as a discipline.
quests.correctAnswer: So valuable is the skill of asking a genuinely good question that entire fields now teach it as a discipline.

quests.hint: 'Oddly enough' is inserted mid-sentence, signalling a mildly surprising claim.
quests.explanation: 'Oddly enough' inserted mid-sentence softens a claim that might otherwise seem too bold. 'Open doors' returns from earlier in this course, again meaning to create opportunities.
quests.textToSpeak: Curiosity, oddly enough, often opens more doors than confidence does, even though confidence tends to get all the credit.
quests.correctAnswer: Curiosity, oddly enough, often opens more doors than confidence does, even though confidence tends to get all the credit.

quests.hint: 'None of this suggests that... only that...' carefully limits and refines a claim.
quests.explanation: This structure carefully limits a claim, first ruling out a misreading, then offering the more precise, intended meaning. 'Fragile' here is used figuratively, describing something easily lost or broken, like certainty.
quests.textToSpeak: None of this suggests that certainty is worthless, only that it's rarer, and more fragile, than most people would like to admit.
quests.correctAnswer: None of this suggests that certainty is worthless, only that it's rarer, and more fragile, than most people would like to admit.

quests.hint: 'What ties... together' works as the subject of this closing, summarising sentence.
quests.explanation: 'Tie together' figuratively describes connecting separate ideas into a coherent whole, a natural verb for a closing, summarising sentence. 'Tidy' here means neat and simple, the opposite of complicated or messy.
quests.textToSpeak: What ties most of these ideas together is a simple reminder that things are rarely as tidy as they first appear.
quests.correctAnswer: What ties most of these ideas together is a simple reminder that things are rarely as tidy as they first appear.

quests.hint: 'However confident' is inserted mid-sentence, conceding a point before the main claim.
quests.explanation: 'However confident' inserted mid-sentence concedes that some people appear certain, before undercutting that appearance with the sentence's real point. This reflective closing captures a fittingly humble note to end this level on.
quests.textToSpeak: Perhaps the most honest thing anyone can say about the future is simply that nobody, however confident, actually knows for certain.
quests.correctAnswer: Perhaps the most honest thing anyone can say about the future is simply that nobody, however confident, actually knows for certain.
